about: Justification trainer prompts for Unit 1 (docs/apphys-architecture.md, "Justification trainer").

prompts.title: What a straight position graph says
prompts.context: A cart moves along a straight track. Its position-time graph is a straight line from x = 2.0 m at t = 0 to x = 10.0 m at t = 4.0 s.
prompts.prompt: Determine the cart's velocity, and justify whether the cart is speeding up.
checklist: Uses the slope of the position-time graph as the velocity: (10.0 m − 2.0 m) / 4.0 s = 2.0 m/s
Says the slope is the same everywhere because the graph is a straight line
Concludes the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the cart is not speeding up

earns.answer: The velocity is the slope of the position-time graph: (10.0 m − 2.0 m) / (4.0 s − 0) = 2.0 m/s. The graph is a straight line, so its slope, and with it the velocity, is the same at every instant. A constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the cart is not speeding up even though its position keeps increasing.
earns.why: It reads the right feature of the graph (the slope, not the height), gives the value with its unit, and links a constant slope to a constant velocity.

misses.answer: The cart is speeding up, because its position keeps getting larger as time goes on.
misses.why: A growing position only means the cart moves forward. Speeding up would need a slope that gets steeper; this answer reads the height of the graph instead of its slope.

prompts.title: Displacement from a velocity graph
prompts.context: A runner starts from rest. Her velocity-time graph rises in a straight line from 0 to 6.0 m/s over the first 3.0 s, then stays flat at 6.0 m/s from 3.0 s to 6.0 s.
prompts.prompt: Calculate her displacement from t = 0 to t = 6.0 s, and explain how you used the graph.
checklist: Uses the area between the velocity-time graph and the time axis as the displacement
Splits the area into a triangle, ½(3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 9.0 m, and a rectangle, (3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 18 m
Adds them: 27 m, with the unit

earns.answer: The displacement is the area between the velocity-time graph and the time axis. From 0 to 3.0 s the area is a triangle, ½(3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 9.0 m. From 3.0 s to 6.0 s it is a rectangle, (3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 18 m. The displacement is 9.0 m + 18 m = 27 m.
earns.why: It names the graph feature (area), handles the part where the velocity is changing, and gives a value with its unit.

misses.answer: Displacement = velocity × time = (6.0 m/s)(6.0 s) = 36 m.
misses.why: This treats the velocity as 6.0 m/s the whole time. During the first 3.0 s she is slower than that, so the area under the rising part is a triangle, not a rectangle.

prompts.title: Which ball lands first
prompts.context: From the same height above level ground, at the same instant, one ball is dropped from rest and an identical ball is launched horizontally at 8.0 m/s. Air resistance is negligible.
prompts.prompt: Predict which ball reaches the ground first, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Claims they land at the same time
Says the horizontal and vertical motions are independent, so the horizontal speed does not change the vertical motion
Both start with zero vertical velocity, have the same downward acceleration g and fall the same height, so h = ½gt² gives the same t = √(2h/g) for both

earns.answer: They land at the same time. The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent. Vertically, both balls start with zero velocity, both have the same downward acceleration g, and both fall the same height h, so h = ½gt² gives the same time t = √(2h/g) for each. The launched ball's 8.0 m/s horizontal velocity does not appear in this equation; it only carries that ball farther from the starting point.
earns.why: It makes the claim, names the independence of the two motions, and shows from the vertical equation that the horizontal speed cannot change the time.

misses.answer: The dropped ball lands first, because it travels a shorter distance than the ball that moves sideways.
misses.why: The time to land depends only on the vertical motion. The launched ball does go farther, but sideways, and that does not slow its fall.

prompts.title: Measure a cart's acceleration
prompts.context: You have a cart, a long ramp, a meterstick, a stopwatch and tape for marking the ramp. The cart is released from rest and speeds up with constant acceleration down the ramp.
prompts.prompt: Describe a procedure to find the cart's acceleration, including what you would graph and how you would use the graph.
checklist: Releases the cart from rest at a marked start, with the meterstick measuring the distance d to several finish marks
Times each run with the stopwatch, repeating each distance several times and averaging to reduce uncertainty
Graphs d against t² (from d = ½at² for a start from rest), draws a best-fit straight line, and uses a = 2 × slope

earns.answer: Mark a start line and five finish lines at different distances d down the ramp, measuring each d with the meterstick. Release the cart from rest at the start line and time how long it takes to reach a finish line with the stopwatch; do three trials for each distance and average the times. Because the cart starts from rest with constant acceleration, d = ½at². So graph d (vertical) against t² (horizontal), draw the best-fit straight line, and find its slope: the slope is a/2, so a = 2 × slope.
earns.why: It names each measured quantity with its instrument, repeats trials, chooses a graph that is a straight line, and says how its slope gives the acceleration.

misses.answer: Roll the cart down the ramp and time it with the stopwatch. Then the acceleration is a = v/t.
misses.why: It never says what distance is measured or how, uses one run, and v is not measured at all. The readers want measured quantities, instruments, repeats and how the graph gives the answer.
